01.note: Rav Yosef bar Ḥama used to seize the slaves of people who owed him money and put them to work. His son Rava asked why. He cited Rav Naḥman: a slave is not worth even the bread he eats, so the owners lost nothing. Rava said Rav Naḥman meant idle slaves like his own slave Dari, who only dances among the wine barrels. His father then cited Rav: one who seizes another's slave and works him owes nothing, since the owner is glad the slave keeps working. Rava replied that this holds only when no money is owed; for a creditor it looks like interest. His father said: I retract.
01.why: The Gemara has just cited Rav Naḥman's ruling that a lender living in his borrower's courtyard must pay rent, so the stay does not look like interest. Rava uses that same ruling to show his father that working a debtor's slaves is the same problem.

people.name: Rav Yosef bar Ḥama
people.about: Rava's father, who seized the slaves of his debtors and made them work for him.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rav Yosef bar Ḥama's son, who questions his father's practice and persuades him to stop.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Sage whose rulings both father and son cite.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Sage who ruled that one who seizes another's slave and works him is exempt.

people.name: Dari
people.about: Rav Naḥman's slave, who only dances among the wine barrels.

terms.meaning: Jewish law forbids a lender to take any benefit from a borrower beyond the loan itself; even a benefit that only looks like payment for the loan is forbidden.
Jewish law; the binding ruling on a question.

02.note: A man sold land with a guarantee to compensate the buyer if the seller's creditors ever took it. The buyer asked to be repaid, in that case, from the seller's very best land; the seller refused, wanting to keep it, but promised his other good land. In the end creditors seized the field, and a flood swept away the seller's very best land, leaving the other good land as his best. Rav Pappa thought the seller must still pay from the good land he had promised. Rav Aḥa of Difti asked Ravina why the seller could not say his promise assumed his best land would still exist, and that his good land had now taken its place. The text gives no final ruling.
02.why: Just before this, Rav Pappa ruled on land set aside to repay a debt. Here he again judges what a specific promise of land for repayment obligates, and his view is challenged.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Sage who thought the seller must keep his promise and pay from his good land.

people.name: Rav Aḥa of Difti
people.about: Sage who argued to Ravina that the seller could refuse.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Sage to whom Rav Aḥa of Difti put his argument.

terms.meaning: Jewish law grades land as best, middle and poorest. Normally a buyer whose land is seized is compensated from the seller's middle-quality land, so a promise of better land matters.
A seller's commitment to repay the buyer if the seller's creditors later seize the land he sold.

03.note: A group of ice plant dealers took turns baking for one another. One day the others asked one of them to bake when it was not his turn, and he said: in payment for my baking, guard my cloak. Before he came back, the cloak was stolen. Rav Pappa ruled that they must pay for it. The Sages objected that this was guarding while the owner was working for them, which would excuse them, and Rav Pappa was embarrassed. Then it came out that at that time the cloak's owner had been drinking beer, not baking.
03.why: The discussion is about when guardians are excused because the owner was working for them. The Gemara retells this case to explain Rav Pappa's embarrassment even under the view that carelessness is never excused: baking out of turn made the dealers paid guardians.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Judge who ruled the dealers liable for the stolen cloak.

terms.meaning: A rule that a guardian is not liable for loss if the owner of the item was working for him at the time.
Someone paid, in money or in kind, to guard another's property. A paid guardian must pay for theft or loss, unlike an unpaid one.

04.note: As young men, Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi sat on the ground before the leading Sages, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa. Their sharp questions and answers led the Sages to give them benches. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi's father, protested that they were taking his only fledgling from him, so Rabbi was sent back to the floor; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa had Rabbi Elazar, who had no father to speak for him, sent back too. Rabbi Elazar was offended at being made Rabbi's equal, and from then on he knocked down Rabbi's arguments before he could make them. Rabbi complained to his father, who said: he is a lion son of a lion, and you are a lion son of a fox.
04.why: Rabbi Elazar's widow has just told Rabbi she did not know whether her husband was greater than him in Torah; the Gemara tells this to show that he was. It also explains why Rabbi named his father among three truly modest people.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Brilliant young scholar, raised to a bench and then sent back to the floor.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; son of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, seated with Rabbi Elazar as a young man.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: Leading Sage and Rabbi's father, who called himself a fox.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa
people.about: Leading Sage who argued that Rabbi Elazar should be sent back to the floor too.

people.name: Jonathan, son of Saul
people.about: Named by Rabbi as modest, for telling David he would be second to him.

terms.meaning: Used alone, this title means Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
A family who led the Sages and, as the Gemara says, seated Hillel at their head and appointed him Nasi over themselves.
The title of the head of the Sages.

05.note: Rabbi Ḥanina and Rabbi Ḥiyya used to argue over Torah. Rabbi Ḥanina told Rabbi Ḥiyya he was no match for him: if the Torah were ever forgotten, he could restore it by his reasoning alone. Rabbi Ḥiyya answered that he was the one making sure it would never be forgotten. He sows flax, twines nets, hunts deer and feeds their meat to orphans, makes parchment from the hides and writes the five books of the Torah on it. Then he goes to a town, teaches five children one book each and six children one order of the Mishna each, and tells them to teach one another until he comes back.
05.why: Just before this, a Divine Voice told Reish Lakish that he had studied Torah like Rabbi Ḥiyya but had not spread it as he did. This exchange shows what that spreading looked like, and the discussion goes on praising Rabbi Ḥiyya.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: Sage who boasted he could restore the Torah by his reasoning if it were forgotten.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Sage who made sure the Torah would not be forgotten by teaching children himself.

terms.meaning: The five books of Moses: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy.
The Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law, is divided into six sections called orders.

06.note: Ifera Hurmiz, mother of King Shapur of Persia, sent four hundred dinars to Rabbi Ami, who refused them, and then to Rava, who accepted them to keep peace with the kingdom. Rabbi Ami was angry. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Ami thought Rava should have given the money to poor gentiles rather than poor Jews, and in fact Rava had done just that. Rabbi Ami was angry only because the people who told him the story had not told it to the end.
06.why: The Sages have been debating whether charity given by non-Jewish nations earns them merit. This incident shows two Sages facing the question in practice, when a Persian queen sends a gift.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Sage who refused the queen's gift and was angry that Rava accepted it.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage who accepted the gift to keep peace with the kingdom and gave it to poor gentiles.

terms.meaning: A person who is not Jewish.
Keeping good relations with the ruling power, here the Persian king's court.

06.flag: The STORY segments hold only the Gemara's follow-up explanation; the incident itself (the queen's gift, Rabbi Ami's refusal, Rava's acceptance) is in the BEFORE segment just preceding.

07.note: Two people each claimed a piece of land had belonged to their ancestors. The first brought witnesses that it had been his ancestors' and that he had worked it for the years needed to establish ownership; the second brought witnesses only that he had worked it for those years. Rav Naḥman ruled that the two testimonies about working the land cancel each other out, leaving the testimony about the ancestors, so the land stays with the first man. Rava objected that the first man's witnesses had been contradicted. Rav Naḥman answered that they were contradicted only about working the land, not about whose ancestors owned it.
07.why: The Gemara next asks whether Rav Naḥman and Rava are repeating an older dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Ḥisda: whether witnesses contradicted by other witnesses may still be believed.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Judge who awarded the land to the man whose ancestors' ownership went unchallenged.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage who objected that contradicted witnesses cannot be relied on.

terms.meaning: If someone openly works land and eats its produce for the required number of years without protest, the court presumes he owns it.

08.note: A man challenged another's hold on a field: what do you want with this land? The holder said he had bought it from him and showed a bill of sale. The first man said the bill was forged. The holder leaned over and whispered to Rabba: yes, it is forged, but I had a real bill that was lost, so I kept this one in hand for whatever it was worth. Rabba reasoned that the man had no reason to lie, since he could simply have claimed the bill was genuine. Rav Yosef objected: what are you relying on, this bill? An admitted forgery is just a worthless shard.
08.why: Rav Idi bar Avin rules right after this that in land cases the law follows Rabba, so the land stays with the man holding it. A matching case about a forged loan note follows, where the law goes the other way.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Judge who believed the holder, since he could have lied more easily.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who objected that a forged bill proves nothing.

terms.meaning: A written deed, signed by witnesses, recording the purchase of land.

09.note: A man demanded a hundred dinars from another and showed a promissory note. The other said the note was forged. The lender leaned over and whispered to Rava: yes, it is forged, but I had a real note that was lost, so I kept this one in hand for whatever it was worth. Rabba reasoned that the man had no reason to lie, since he could simply have claimed the note was genuine. Rav Yosef objected that an admitted forgery is just a worthless shard and cannot be relied on.
09.why: It mirrors the forged bill of sale case just before. Rav Idi bar Avin then rules that with money the law follows Rav Yosef, so the money stays with the alleged borrower, unlike the land case.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge to whom the lender whispered his admission.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Sage who reasoned the lender had no reason to lie.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who objected that a forged note proves nothing.

terms.meaning: A written document recording a loan, which the lender can use to collect the debt in court.
A silver coin.

09.flag: The man whispers to Rava but Rabba answers; in the matching case just before it is Rabba throughout, so the name may be a scribal variant.

10.note: Abaye offered to show Rava how the swindlers of Pumbedita operate. An owner asks a craftsman for his cloak back, and the craftsman says it never happened. The owner says he has witnesses who saw it with him; the craftsman says that was a different cloak. The owner says: bring it out and let us look. The craftsman says: I will not bring it out. Rava answered that the craftsman's claim holds, because the teaching on this speaks of an owner who saw his own cloak there.
10.why: The Gemara is discussing items left with craftsmen and when an owner can reclaim them. Rava reads the earlier teaching as requiring that the owner actually saw his item; Rav Ashi then shows how a clever owner can meet that test.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who describes the trick of the swindlers of Pumbedita.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage who holds that the craftsman's claim is valid.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.
A town in Babylonia.

11.note: After the Second Temple was destroyed, many Jews stopped eating meat and drinking wine, because both had been offered on the altar, which was gone. Rabbi Yehoshua asked: then should we not eat bread, since the meal-offerings have ceased? They said they could live on other produce. Nor fruit, since the first fruits have ceased? Other fruit, they said. Nor water, since the water libation has ceased? They fell silent. He told them: not to mourn at all is impossible, but to mourn too much is also impossible, since the Sages impose only what most people can bear. Instead, plaster your house but leave a small patch bare; prepare a meal but leave out a small item; a woman may adorn herself but leave out one small thing.
11.why: The discussion has just taught that one may not fully plaster a house, as mourning for the Temple. This teaching shows where that limited practice comes from: Rabbi Yehoshua's answer to people who wanted to mourn far more.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Sage who argued with the ascetics and set limits on mourning.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who said the bare patch should be one cubit by one cubit.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Sage who said the bare patch should face the entrance.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Sage who said the item left out of a meal is like small fried fish.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Sage who said a woman leaves some hair at her temple unremoved.

terms.meaning: People who deny themselves ordinary pleasures; here, those who gave up meat and wine in mourning.
Offerings of flour brought on the Temple altar.
The first ripe produce, which farmers brought to the Temple.
Water poured on the Temple altar as an offering.

12.note: Rabbi Yehuda told of a man in Tzalmon who planted his vineyard with rows sixteen cubits apart. He bent the branches of each pair of rows to one side and sowed the cleared ground, switching sides the next year. The case came before the Sages and they permitted it. Rav Yosef answered that he did not know about this, but recalled a case in a village of shepherds: Rav Yehuda told a man who had sold trees to give the buyer enough land for an ox and its gear. Rav Yosef did not know how much that was until he learned that a tree must be planted four cubits from a neighbor's field, to leave room for work, and concluded that it meant four cubits.
12.why: The Gemara is asking how far apart trees may stand and still count as one unit, so the buyer gets the land under them. Abaye cites the Tzalmon case for the sixteen-cubit view; Rav Yosef answers with Rav Yehuda's ruling to back his smaller figure.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Sage who reports the Tzalmon vineyard case.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who answers with a case he witnessed and works out its meaning.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Judge who told the seller to give enough land for an ox and its gear.

terms.meaning: An ancient measure of length, roughly the length of a forearm.
A teaching from the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

12.flag: Two separate incidents are joined: the Tzalmon vineyard (cited by Abaye) and Rav Yehuda's ruling in the village of shepherds (cited by Rav Yosef against him).

13.note: Issur, a convert, had twelve thousand dinars deposited with Rava. His son Rav Mari was conceived before Issur converted but born after, and was away at a study hall when Issur lay dying. Rava reasoned that Rav Mari had no way to get the money: not by inheritance, since such a son does not inherit; not as a deathbed gift, which follows inheritance rules; and not by any formal act of acquisition, since the coins were not with Issur, he had no land, and Rava would not come if sent for. Rav Ika, son of Rav Ami, asked why Issur could not admit the money was Rav Mari's. Meanwhile a written admission came out of Issur's house. Rava was angry: they are teaching people claims and causing me a loss.
13.why: The Sages have asked whether a dying man's admission that he owes money counts as valid. The Gemara brings this incident as proof that it does: Issur's written admission secured the money for his son.

people.name: Issur the convert
people.about: A convert who had money deposited with Rava and lay dying.

people.name: Rav Mari
people.about: Issur's son, conceived before his father converted and born after.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage holding Issur's money, who expected to keep it.

people.name: Rav Ika, son of Rav Ami
people.about: Sage who pointed out that Issur could simply admit the money was his son's.

terms.meaning: A person who has formally joined the Jewish people.

terms.term: gift of a person on his deathbed
terms.meaning: The Sages let a dying person give property away by word alone, but such a gift follows the rules of inheritance.
A formal act, such as handing over an object, that transfers ownership; it does not work for coins.

14.note: In Bnei Brak a man sold part of the property he had inherited from his father, and then died. His relatives challenged the sale, saying he had still been a minor when he died. They asked Rabbi Akiva whether they might examine the body. He said they were not permitted to disgrace him, and besides, the signs of puberty tend to change after death.
14.why: The Sages disagree whether an heir may sell his father's property at eighteen or only at twenty. Rabbi Zeira cites this case against the view of twenty: a twenty-year-old counts as an adult anyway, so examining the body would prove nothing.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Sage who forbade examining the dead man's body.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Sage who cites the case to challenge one view of the age of sale.

terms.meaning: Someone who has not reached legal adulthood; his sale of inherited land is not valid.
Physical signs, such as body hair, by which Jewish law marks a young man as an adult.

15.note: A deed of gift came before Rav Yosef signed by two witnesses who were brothers-in-law. He wanted to accept it, since Shmuel had ruled that the law follows Rabbi Yosei, whom he understood to allow brothers-in-law. Abaye asked how he knew Shmuel meant that version of Rabbi Yosei's view, and the two argued over what Shmuel meant when he said he and his brother Pineḥas could not testify together. Rav Yosef then told the holder to take possession through the witnesses who saw the deed handed over. When Abaye objected that even then a deed with invalid signatures is invalid, Rav Yosef told the man: go, the rabbis will not let me give it to you.
15.why: The discussion is about which in-laws may not serve as witnesses, and has just cited Shmuel's ruling that the law follows Rabbi Yosei. Rav Yosef tries to apply it, and Abaye shows that it is unclear which version of Rabbi Yosei's view Shmuel meant.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who first wanted to accept the deed and finally sent its holder away.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who challenged each of Rav Yosef's reasons.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Sage whose ruling on Rabbi Yosei is in question.

people.name: Pineḥas
people.about: Shmuel's brother, also his brother-in-law.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Early Sage whose view on brothers-in-law as witnesses is debated.

terms.meaning: A document recording that property was given as a gift, signed by two witnesses.
In Rabbi Elazar's view a document takes effect through the witnesses who see it handed over, not those who sign it.
Here, men married to two sisters.

16.note: The descendants of Ishmael and of Keturah took the Jewish people to judgment before Alexander of Macedon, claiming a share of the land of Canaan, since the Torah calls both Ishmael and Isaac sons of Abraham. Geviha ben Pesisa asked the Sages' leave to argue: if he lost, they could say only an ordinary man was beaten; if he won, that the Torah of Moses had won. He asked his opponents for their proof; they said: the Torah. He answered from the Torah: Abraham gave all he had to Isaac, gave gifts to his concubines' sons and sent them away. A son sent away by a father who divided his property in his lifetime has no claim on the other. The outcome is not told here.
16.why: This is one of a series of cases in which Geviha ben Pesisa argued for the Jews before Alexander; just before, he answered the Egyptians' claim by demanding wages for the years of slavery in Egypt.

people.name: Geviha ben Pesisa
people.about: Argues for the Jewish people before Alexander, with the Sages' permission.

people.name: Alexander of Macedon
people.about: The ruler before whom the case is brought.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
people.about: Sage who explains what Abraham's gifts to the concubines' sons were.

terms.meaning: A wife of Abraham; her sons were among those he sent away with gifts.
A deed by which a father divides his property among his sons during his lifetime.

17.note: Rabbi Yoḥanan taught that God will one day set gems thirty cubits square, with openings bored through them, as the gates of Jerusalem. A student mocked him: we cannot even find a gem the size of a dove's egg. Later, at sea, the student saw ministering angels cutting such stones, and they told him they were for the gates of Jerusalem. Back home he told Rabbi Yoḥanan: teach, master, it is fitting for you to teach; I saw just what you said. Rabbi Yoḥanan answered: good-for-nothing, had you not seen it, you would not have believed? You mock the words of the Sages. He set his eyes on him and turned him into a pile of bones.
17.why: Rabbi Yirmeya asked whether an elder's praise of a Sage's teaching was disrespect. Rabbi Zeira says no, it was support; real disrespect is this student's, who agreed with Rabbi Yoḥanan only once he had seen it for himself.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Sage whose teaching about the gates of Jerusalem the student mocked.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Tells this story in answer to Rabbi Yirmeya's question.

terms.meaning: The angels who serve God.
An ancient measure of length, roughly the length of a forearm.

18.note: When Rabbi Eliezer fell ill, his students came to visit. He said there was fierce wrath in the world. They wept; Rabbi Akiva laughed. As long as his teacher's wine, flax, oil and honey never spoiled, Akiva said, he feared Rabbi Eliezer had already received all his reward; now, seeing him suffer, he was glad. Asked whether he had neglected any of the Torah, Akiva quoted his teacher's own lesson: no one on earth is so righteous that he never sins. In a second account, four Sages visit. Three praise him as better for Israel than rain, the sun, or parents; Akiva says suffering is precious. Rabbi Eliezer asks to be propped up to hear, and Akiva proves it from King Manasseh, whom only suffering turned back to God.
18.why: Just before, a verse is read to say that even when God brings illness, He heals. These visits to the sick Rabbi Eliezer turn to the value of suffering, and the discussion then follows Manasseh's repentance.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: Sage who fell ill and was visited by his students and colleagues.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's student, who laughed at his illness and taught that suffering is precious.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: Visitor who called Rabbi Eliezer better for Israel than rain.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Visitor who called Rabbi Eliezer better for Israel than the sun.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: Visitor who called Rabbi Eliezer better for Israel than a father and mother.

terms.meaning: Got his whole reward in this life, leaving none for the World-to-Come.
The life after this one, where the righteous are rewarded.

19.note: Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva went up to Jerusalem after the Temple was destroyed. At Mount Scopus they tore their clothes, and on the Temple Mount they saw a fox come out of the place of the Holy of Holies. The others wept and Akiva laughed. They said: of this place it is written that an outsider who approaches shall die, and now foxes walk in it; shall we not weep? He answered that Scripture links Uriah's prophecy that Zion would be plowed like a field with Zechariah's that old men and women would again sit in Jerusalem's streets. Now that the first has come true, the second surely will. They said: Akiva, you have comforted us.
19.why: It follows an earlier journey of the same Sages, when Rabbi Akiva laughed at the noise of Rome while they wept. Both carry the discussion's theme of exile and hope for redemption, and this story closes the tractate.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Sage who laughs at the ruined Temple and comforts his colleagues.

people.name: Uriah the priest
people.about: Prophet who foretold that Zion would be plowed as a field.

people.name: Zechariah the son of Jeberechiah
people.about: Prophet who foretold that old men and women would again sit in Jerusalem.

terms.meaning: The innermost chamber of the Temple, the most sacred place in it.
A hill from which travelers first saw the site of the Temple.
The hill in Jerusalem on which the Temple stood.

20.note: A lender told a borrower: when you repay me, do it in front of two people who have learned halakha. The borrower repaid him privately, with no one present, and the coins were then taken by forces beyond the lender's control. The lender came before Rav Naḥman: yes, I took the money, but only as a deposit to hold until two learned people came along and the condition could be met, so the loss is not mine. Rav Naḥman said that since he admitted taking it, it was a full repayment. And if he wanted the condition met, let him bring the money now, since Rav Naḥman and Rav Sheshet had learned halakha, Sifra, Sifrei, Tosefta and the whole Talmud.
20.why: The Gemara is collecting cases about repaying loans before witnesses. Just before, Rava ruled that a lender who names particular witnesses can insist on them; here Rav Naḥman holds that money the lender admits receiving is repaid regardless.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Judge who held that the debt had been repaid.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: Sage named by Rav Naḥman as fully learned, along with himself.

terms.meaning: Jewish law.
Early collections of the Sages' teachings, studied alongside the Mishna.
Property held for safekeeping. An unpaid keeper is not liable when it is lost through forces beyond his control.
